content.text: {"primary_meaning":"A preliminary, incomplete foreshadowing or type of the greater spiritual reality fulfilled in Christ. Christian interpretation especially describes the Mosaic law, sacrifices, festivals, priesthood, and earthly sanctuary as “shadows,” while Christ and the new-covenant realities are the substance.","primary_basis":["Colossians 2:16–17 — food laws, festivals, new moons, and Sabbaths are “a shadow of the things to come,” while the substance belongs to Christ.","Hebrews 8:4–5 — the earthly priests and sanctuary serve “a copy and shadow of the heavenly things.”","Hebrews 10:1 — the law has “a shadow of the good things to come” rather than their full reality.","Hebrews 9:23–24 — the earthly sanctuary is treated as a copy of the heavenly reality, supporting the same shadow-and-fulfillment framework."],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"Divine protection, refuge, and nearness, especially being sheltered under the shadow of God’s wings.","basis":["Psalm 17:8","Psalm 36:7","Psalm 57:1","Psalm 63:7","Psalm 91:1","Isaiah 32:2"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Mortality, transience, or the fleeting and insubstantial character of human life.","basis":["1 Chronicles 29:15","Job 8:9","Job 14:2","Psalm 102:11","Psalm 109:23","Psalm 144:4","Ecclesiastes 6:12"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Deep darkness, mortal danger, suffering, or death, traditionally expressed as “the shadow of death.”","basis":["Job 3:5","Job 10:21–22","Psalm 23:4","Psalm 44:19","Psalm 107:10","Isaiah 9:2; compare Matthew 4:16 and Luke 1:79"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Change, instability, or variation, used negatively of God, with whom there is no shifting shadow.","basis":["James 1:17"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"A vehicle or sign of extraordinary apostolic healing power, based on people hoping Peter’s shadow would fall on the sick.","basis":["Acts 5:15–16"],"prominence":"rare"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"high","notes":"There is a settled dominant theological use of “shadow” in Christian typology: an anticipatory and inferior form that points to fulfillment in Christ. The word is nevertheless context-dependent across Scripture and does not carry that meaning in every occurrence; protection, transience, and death or danger are also well-established biblical metaphors."}
